questions.stem: An 81 year old woman with atrial fibrillation, who stopped warfarin after a fall, had sudden severe pain in her left leg 40 minutes ago while watching television. The leg is white and cold from mid-calf down, and she has pins and needles in her foot. No pulses are palpable below the femoral artery. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm irregular.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden pain, pallor, cold, pulseless and paraesthesia over minutes in a patient in AF off anticoagulation is acute limb ischaemia from embolism.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
Minutes of onset plus the Ps (pain, pallor, perishingly cold, pulseless, paraesthesia) with an embolic source.

elim: Develops over weeks to months with rest pain and ulcers, not over minutes.
Gives a warm, swollen, red leg with intact pulses.
Gives dermatomal pain and paraesthesia with a warm, well-perfused leg.
Causes calf pain and swelling with normal pulses.

steps.x: Acute limb ischaemia: onset over minutes, 6 Ps; AF embolism is a common cause.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has a 2 hour history of sudden pain in his right leg. His foot is pale and perishingly cold. He cannot feel his popliteal or foot pulses on the right, and the left leg is normal. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which other finding is most likely on examination of the right leg?
o: Dependent rubor with a slow capillary refill
Reduced sensation over the dorsum of the foot
questions.e: The 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia are pain, perishingly cold, pulseless, pallor, paraesthesia and paralysis, so altered sensation is expected.

steps.x: The question asks: which other finding is most likely on examination of the right leg?

clues: cannot feel his popliteal or foot pulses
steps.x: Pain, pallor, cold and pulseless are given; the remaining Ps are paraesthesia and paralysis.

elim: He is pulseless below the femoral; the foot pulses are absent.
A sign of chronic, long-standing ischaemia.
Suggests venous or cardiac disease, not acute arterial occlusion.
Typical of DVT or cellulitis.

steps.x: 6 Ps: pain, perishingly cold, pulseless, pallor, paraesthesia, paralysis.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man who smokes 30 cigarettes a day has a 1 year history of aching in both buttocks and thighs after walking 150 metres, relieved by a few minutes' rest. He has also noticed erectile dysfunction. Both femoral pulses are weak and there are no pulses palpable distally.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely to be occluded?
o: Distal aorta and common iliac arteries
questions.e: Bilateral buttock and thigh claudication with weak femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction is aortoiliac occlusion.

steps.x: The question asks: which artery is most likely to be occluded?
Buttock pain means the occlusion is above the femoral; both sides and impotence means aortoiliac.

elim: Gives thigh claudication with a normal femoral pulse.
Gives calf or foot claudication.
Gives calf claudication with a palpable femoral pulse.
Give foot claudication, common in diabetes.

steps.x: Aortoiliac occlusion: claudication of buttocks and thighs (with impotence and weak femoral pulses).

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has a 6 month history of cramping pain in her left calf after walking 200 metres, which goes when she stops. Her left femoral pulse is normal but her left popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent. Her left foot is cooler than the right.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely to be occluded?
questions.e: Calf claudication with a palpable femoral pulse but absent popliteal pulse localises the occlusion to the femoral-popliteal segment, which gives pain below the knee.

steps.x: The question asks: which artery is most likely to be occluded?

clues: popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent
steps.x: Pain one level below the block: femoral present, popliteal absent, calf pain.

elim: Occlusion would remove the femoral pulse and give pain below the inguinal ligament.
Gives buttock and thigh claudication with a weak femoral pulse.
Gives thigh pain, not calf pain.
Gives pain just above the inguinal ligament with a weak femoral pulse.

steps.x: Femoral-popliteal occlusion: pain below the knee (calf). Chronic occlusion: gradual claudication, cold limb, absent pulses.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man had a femoral angiogram through his right groin 3 days ago. He now has sudden pain beginning just below his right inguinal ligament and extending down the whole leg. His right femoral pulse cannot be felt, though the left is strong. His right leg is pale and cold.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely to be occluded?
questions.e: Pain starting below the inguinal ligament with loss of the femoral pulse after groin puncture is common femoral artery occlusion.

steps.x: The question asks: which artery is most likely to be occluded?

clues: just below his right inguinal ligament
right femoral pulse cannot be felt
steps.x: The level of pain and the first missing pulse point to the common femoral artery.

elim: Would affect both legs and remove both femoral pulses.
Isolated occlusion gives thigh pain with a palpable common femoral pulse.
Gives pain just above the inguinal ligament.
Gives foot pain only, with a normal femoral pulse.

steps.x: Common femoral occlusion: pain below the inguinal ligament.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man who smokes has a 4 month history of aching pain in the front and inner part of his right thigh when walking uphill, relieved by rest. He has no buttock or calf pain. His femoral, popliteal and foot pulses are all palpable at rest. Duplex ultrasound shows a stenosis in a branch of the femoral artery.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely to be occluded?
questions.e: Isolated thigh claudication with preserved distal pulses suggests deep femoral (profunda femoris) disease, which supplies the thigh muscles.

steps.x: The question asks: which artery is most likely to be occluded?

clues: a branch of the femoral artery
steps.x: Thigh only, distal pulses fine: the branch that supplies the thigh, the profunda femoris.

elim: Gives buttock and thigh pain with a weak femoral pulse.
Gives calf pain with an absent popliteal pulse.
Gives calf pain because it supplies the leg below the knee.
Gives calf and foot pain.

steps.x: Deep femoral occlusion: thigh pain.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with a history of smoking has a 3 month history of pain just above her left inguinal ligament and in her lower abdomen on walking, relieved by rest. Her left femoral pulse is weak, with a bruit heard just above the groin. Her right leg pulses are normal.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely to be occluded?
questions.e: Unilateral pain just above the inguinal ligament, a weak femoral pulse and a bruit above the groin localise to the external iliac artery.

steps.x: The question asks: which artery is most likely to be occluded?

clues: just above her left inguinal ligament
Her right leg pulses are normal
steps.x: One side only and pain above the groin crease: the vessel just above the inguinal ligament.

elim: Gives pain below the inguinal ligament.
Gives thigh pain with a normal femoral pulse.
Gives bilateral buttock and thigh claudication.
Gives calf pain with a normal femoral pulse.

steps.x: External iliac occlusion: pain just above the inguinal ligament.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man who is an ex-smoker with hypertension attends his GP for a blood pressure review. He has no abdominal or back pain. On examination there is a 5 cm mass just above the umbilicus which pulsates and expands laterally under the examiner's fingers. His BP is 148/90 mmHg and pulse rate 72 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An expansile (not just transmitted) pulsatile mass above the umbilicus in an asymptomatic older male smoker is an abdominal aortic aneurysm.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
Expansile means the mass itself pulses outward, so it is the aorta.

elim: An epigastric mass is hard and does not expand with each pulse.
Is not expansile and is usually found on imaging.
Follows pancreatitis and transmits pulsation but is not expansile.
Is indentable and not pulsatile.

steps.x: AAA: often asymptomatic, pulsatile expansile abdominal mass, with risk of rupture.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man collapses at a bus stop with sudden severe abdominal pain going through to his back. He smokes and has peripheral arterial disease. His pulse rate is 128 bpm, BP 76/44 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. He is pale and sweaty. Urine dipstick shows a trace of blood.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden abdominal and back pain with hypotension and collapse in an older male smoker with arterial disease is a ruptured AAA, which needs emergency surgery.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: abdominal pain going through to his back
steps.x: Older vascular man, pain to the back, shock: ruptured AAA. A trace of blood on dipstick does not mean renal colic.

elim: Gives epigastric pain to the back, but rarely sudden collapse with profound shock at onset.
Gives a rigid abdomen with free gas; back pain and collapse are less typical.
Gives haematuria and loin pain but not shock in a previously well man.
Tearing interscapular back pain with hypertension rather than profound hypotension.

steps.x: AAA rupture: sudden abdominal/back pain + hypotension. Never call it renal colic in an older man first.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man had a large anterior myocardial infarction 2 weeks ago. Echocardiogram showed an akinetic apex. He is in sinus rhythm. He now has sudden severe pain in his right leg, which is pale, cold and pulseless below the groin. He has never had leg pain on walking and his left leg pulses are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his limb ischaemia?
o: Embolism from a left ventricular mural thrombus
Paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale
questions.e: An akinetic apex after anterior MI predisposes to LV mural thrombus; cardiac embolism causes sudden, complete occlusion in a leg without prior claudication.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely cause of his limb ischaemia?

clues: never had leg pain on walking
steps.x: No AF, but a fresh anterior MI with an akinetic apex: a cardiac source of emboli.

elim: Possible after trauma or in the aorta, but there is no tearing pain or trauma.
Needs a venous thrombus crossing a septal defect.
Affects young athletes with exertional calf pain.
Usually follows years of claudication and evolves more slowly.

steps.x: Causes of acute limb ischaemia: AF embolus, thrombosis on PVD, paradoxical and cardiac emboli.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman who smokes has had calf claudication at 100 metres for 3 years. Over the last 12 hours her left foot has become painful at rest, cool and mottled, but she can still move her toes. She is in sinus rhythm. Her right leg pulses are weak and her left foot pulses are absent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her limb ischaemia?
o: Thrombosis on a pre-existing atherosclerotic stenosis
questions.e: Gradual worsening over hours on a background of claudication and bilateral peripheral arterial disease is thrombosis in situ, made less dramatic by collaterals.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely cause of her limb ischaemia?

clues: Her right leg pulses are weak
steps.x: Background PVD, slower onset, no embolic source: in-situ thrombosis.

elim: She is in sinus rhythm, and embolism is sudden and more dramatic.
Gives blue toes with palpable pulses after a procedure.
Gives a warm, swollen leg with pulses present.
Needs a venous thrombus and a septal defect, and is sudden.

steps.x: Thrombosis on PVD presents less dramatically than embolism because collaterals exist.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with a BMI of 41 has a 1 hour history of sudden pain and coldness in his right foot. The foot is pale with reduced sensation. The admitting doctor cannot palpate any foot pulses on either side because of oedema and body habitus. His pulse rate is 110 bpm irregular.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial bedside investigation?
o: Handheld arterial Doppler of the foot vessels
questions.e: A handheld arterial Doppler at the bedside confirms absent or reduced arterial signals in suspected acute limb ischaemia when pulses cannot be felt.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial bedside investigation?
Pulses cannot be assessed by touch, so use the bedside tool that hears arterial flow.

elim: Looks for DVT, not arterial occlusion.
Used to exclude venous thromboembolism.
Not used in an acute cold leg.
Shows bone, not blood flow.

steps.x: Acute limb ischaemia: bedside handheld arterial Doppler first.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has had right calf claudication at 50 metres for a year despite stopping smoking, taking clopidogrel and atorvastatin, and completing supervised exercise. His ABPI is 0.52. The vascular surgeon is considering revascularisation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to plan treatment?
o: CT angiography of the aorta and lower limb arteries
questions.e: CT angiography is the gold standard for chronic occlusion, defining the site and extent of the blockage before angioplasty or bypass.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate investigation to plan treatment?
Best medical therapy has failed; the surgeon needs a map of the arteries.

elim: Screens for AAA, not lower limb occlusions.
Assesses coronary disease, not the site of the leg occlusion.
Confirms disease but does not show its site or extent.
Assesses veins, not arteries.

steps.x: CT angiography is gold standard: defines site and extent of the blockage.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has a 4 month history of left calf pain after walking about 300 metres, which settles within 2 minutes of rest. She has hypertension and smoked for 40 years. Her left foot pulses are weak. Her GP wants to confirm the diagnosis following NICE guidance on peripheral arterial disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Chronic occlusion is confirmed initially with ABPI plus bloods (lipids, HbA1c); NICE PAD guidance recommends ABPI first.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

clues: calf pain after walking about 300 metres
steps.x: Classic gradual claudication: confirm arterial disease at the bedside before imaging.

elim: The gold standard for planning intervention, not the first test.
Assesses venous disease.
For spinal stenosis, which gives pain eased by bending forward rather than standing still.
Assesses muscle damage, not arterial disease.

steps.x: Chronic occlusion: ABPI plus bloods first-line.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man asks his GP for a check-up because his older brother has just had surgery for an abdominal aortic aneurysm. He is an ex-smoker with hypertension. He has no symptoms. The GP thinks she can feel a pulsatile mass but his abdomen is obese.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Ultrasound is first-line for AAA: quick, safe and measures aortic diameter.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
Family history, smoking, a possible pulsatile mass: measure the aorta with ultrasound.

elim: May show calcification but cannot measure the aortic diameter reliably.
Assesses lower limb arterial disease, not the aorta.
Used for planning repair, not first-line.
Assesses the heart and aortic root, not the abdominal aorta.

steps.x: AAA: ultrasound first-line.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has had a cold, pale, pulseless left leg for 4 hours. He is in atrial fibrillation. The vascular team wants a blood test that reflects how much tissue is ischaemic before taking him to theatre. His pulse rate is 112 bpm irregular and BP 138/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate blood test?
questions.e: Raised serum lactate reflects anaerobic metabolism and the degree of tissue ischaemia in acute limb ischaemia.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate blood test?

clues: cold, pale, pulseless left leg for 4 hours
reflects how much tissue is ischaemic
steps.x: Ischaemic muscle switches to anaerobic metabolism and produces lactate.

elim: A non-specific inflammatory marker that rises slowly.
Used to exclude venous thromboembolism.
Used in pancreatitis.
Reflects myocardial injury, not limb ischaemia.

steps.x: Acute limb ischaemia: raised lactate reflects the degree of tissue ischaemia.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman has a 2 hour history of a cold, painful right leg with absent foot pulses. A handheld Doppler gives a weak signal at the ankle. She has chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 16 mL/min/1.73m² and a previous severe reaction to iodinated contrast.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging investigation?
questions.e: Urgent Doppler (duplex) ultrasound shows residual arterial flow and the site of occlusion without contrast when CT angiography is unsafe.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate imaging investigation?

clues: previous severe reaction to iodinated contrast
steps.x: CTA is the gold standard but contrast is off the table; duplex gives flow and site.

elim: Shows nothing about limb arterial flow.
The gold standard, but iodinated contrast is contraindicated here.
Shows bone, not blood flow.
Assesses veins, not arterial flow.

steps.x: Urgent duplex ultrasound demonstrates residual arterial flow; CTA defines site and extent when safe.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman in atrial fibrillation has a 1 hour history of a cold, pale, painful left leg with absent popliteal and foot pulses and reduced sensation. She has been given oxygen, IV fluids and analgesia. The vascular surgeon is on the way.
questions.q: Which drug should be given immediately?
questions.e: IV unfractionated heparin is given immediately in acute limb ischaemia to prevent distal propagation of the thrombus, and is easily reversed before surgery.

steps.x: The question asks: which drug should be given immediately?

clues: The vascular surgeon is on the way
steps.x: Stop the clot growing while surgery is arranged; it must be quick and reversible.

elim: Too slow in onset for acute limb ischaemia; used for long-term AF prevention.
An antiplatelet that does not stop clot propagation.
An antiplatelet for chronic disease, not acute embolic occlusion.
Takes days to work.

steps.x: Acute limb ischaemia: IV unfractionated heparin to prevent thrombus propagation.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man in atrial fibrillation has had a white, cold, pulseless right leg for 2 hours. He has paraesthesia but can still move his toes. CT angiography shows an embolus at the femoral bifurcation. He has had IV unfractionated heparin and has been referred urgently to vascular surgery, following Vascular Society guidance.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Oral anticoagulation and review in clinic
questions.e: An embolic occlusion with a viable limb needs emergency surgical embolectomy within 6 hours to prevent irreversible necrosis.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate definitive management?
Viable leg, within the window, embolic cause: remove the clot now.

elim: For an unsalvageable leg; this leg is still viable.
Used for venous disease and harmful in arterial ischaemia.
Leaves the leg ischaemic beyond the 6-hour window.
Treats chronic claudication.

steps.x: Definitive management: emergency embolectomy within 6 hours.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman arrives in the emergency department with a 90 minute history of a cold, pale, pulseless left leg. She is in severe pain and is distressed. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm irregular, BP 108/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. She looks dry.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Elevate the leg and apply a warm blanket
Oral paracetamol and outpatient vascular clinic
Oxygen, IV fluids, analgesia and urgent vascular surgery referral
questions.e: Acute limb ischaemia is managed with a DR ABCDE approach: oxygen, IV fluids and analgesia, with urgent vascular surgery referral.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial management?
Hypoxic, dry and in pain: ABCDE first, and call vascular early.

elim: Elevation worsens arterial perfusion and warming increases metabolic demand.
Far too slow for a threatened limb.
For chronic disease; this is an emergency.
Not given before vascular assessment and imaging.

steps.x: Acute limb ischaemia: DR ABCDE, O2, IV fluids, analgesia, urgent vascular referral.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has confirmed peripheral arterial disease with an ABPI of 0.72 and calf claudication at 250 metres. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day. His total cholesterol is 5.9 mmol/L. He has no other medical history.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug management?
questions.e: Chronic occlusion is managed with lifestyle modification (smoking cessation, exercise) plus antiplatelets (clopidogrel) and a high-intensity statin, per NICE PAD guidance.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate drug management?
Stable claudication: reduce cardiovascular risk with antiplatelet plus statin and stop smoking.

elim: A diuretic with no role in arterial disease.
Only considered after supervised exercise fails, and does not reduce cardiovascular risk.
Not used to treat claudication.
Anticoagulation is not first-line for stable claudication.

steps.x: Chronic occlusion: lifestyle change, antiplatelets and statins.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 5.8 cm on ultrasound. Six months ago it measured 5.3 cm. He is fit, with no major heart or lung disease. His BP is 136/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Start aspirin and review in 2 years
questions.e: Aneurysms are managed by size: small ones by surveillance and large ones (5.5 cm or more, or rapidly growing) by surgical repair, open or EVAR.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate management?

clues: Six months ago it measured 5.3 cm
steps.x: Large and growing: repair, not surveillance.

elim: A 5.8 cm aneurysm carries a high rupture risk.
Surveillance is for small aneurysms.
Medical therapy alone does not prevent rupture of a large aneurysm.
Has no role in aneurysm management.

steps.x: Aneurysm management by size: small = surveillance, large = repair (EVAR or open).

questions.stem: A 77 year old man with a known 6.1 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm, awaiting repair, develops sudden severe back pain. His pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 82/50 mmHg. He is conscious. Two large-bore cannulas are in place and blood has been sent for crossmatch.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Abdominal ultrasound in the radiology department
Fluid resuscitation to a systolic BP of 140 mmHg
Immediate transfer for emergency aneurysm repair
IV morphine and admit to a ward bed
questions.e: A known large AAA with sudden back pain and hypotension has ruptured and needs emergency surgery without delay for further imaging.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Unstable, known AAA, new pain: rupture. Go to theatre.

elim: Delays theatre; the diagnosis is clinical in an unstable known AAA.
Aggressive fluids worsen bleeding; permissive hypotension is used.
Leaves a ruptured aneurysm untreated.
Rupture is rapidly fatal without surgery.

steps.x: A ruptured aneurysm requires emergency surgery.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with 5 years of calf claudication develops a complete occlusion of his superficial femoral artery on duplex ultrasound. His leg is cool with absent foot pulses but it is not pale, and he has no rest pain or sensory loss. A patient with an embolus to the same artery last week lost sensation within an hour.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason for his milder presentation?
o: Collateral vessels have developed around the chronic stenosis
His leg muscles have less metabolic demand
Superficial femoral occlusion never causes ischaemia
The occlusion is in a vein
questions.e: Thrombosis on chronic atherosclerosis develops slowly, so collaterals have already formed; embolism causes sudden complete occlusion with no time for collaterals, so it is more dramatic.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely reason for his milder presentation?
Same artery, different speed of onset: the slow one had time to build a bypass network.

elim: Viscosity does not explain the difference.
Muscle demand is similar in both patients.
It can cause acute limb ischaemia if collaterals are absent.
The duplex shows an arterial occlusion.

steps.x: Embolic occlusion is dramatic (no collaterals); thrombotic on chronic disease is milder (collaterals).

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman has had acute limb ischaemia of her right leg for 5 hours. Her venous blood gas shows a pH of 7.28 (7.35–7.45), bicarbonate 17 mmol/L (22–29) and lactate 6.4 mmol/L (0.5–2.0). She has not vomited and has no diabetes or sepsis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her raised lactate?
o: Anaerobic metabolism in ischaemic limb muscle
Respiratory failure with carbon dioxide retention
questions.e: Ischaemic tissue without oxygen switches to anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactate; the level reflects the degree of tissue ischaemia.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely mechanism of her raised lactate?

clues: acute limb ischaemia of her right leg for 5 hours
steps.x: The only source is the ischaemic leg.

elim: She has no diabetes, and ketones, not lactate, drive the acidosis in DKA.
No liver disease is described.
She is not taking metformin.
Causes respiratory, not lactic, acidosis.

steps.x: Raised lactate in limb ischaemia = anaerobic metabolism in ischaemic tissue.

questions.stem: An 83 year old man is found on the floor at home. His left leg has been cold and pulseless for at least 10 hours. The calf is hard and tender, the skin shows fixed blue mottling that does not blanch, and he cannot move his foot or feel touch below the knee.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for these findings?
questions.e: Skeletal muscle and peripheral nerves tolerate anaerobic conditions for only about 6 hours; beyond this, fixed mottling, paralysis and a hard calf indicate irreversible necrosis.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely explanation for these findings?

clues: fixed blue mottling that does not blanch
steps.x: Well past the 6-hour window, with fixed staining and paralysis: dead tissue.

elim: Follows revascularisation; this leg has not been reperfused.
Gives a warm, swollen leg with intact pulses.
Blanching mottling and preserved movement are reversible; fixed staining and paralysis are not.
Does not cause a cold, pulseless, mottled limb.

steps.x: 6-hour window = limited anaerobic tolerance of muscle and nerve before irreversible necrosis.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man who has smoked for 50 years and has hypertension has a 5.0 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. He also has calf claudication from a superficial femoral artery occlusion. His son asks how the same man can have one artery that is too wide and another that is blocked.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: A genetic collagen disorder causes both
An embolus from the aneurysm caused the occlusion
Shared risk factors cause different vessel wall responses
The aneurysm diverts blood from the leg
questions.e: Aneurysmal and occlusive disease share risk factors (atherosclerosis, smoking, hypertension) but represent different wall responses: dilation versus stenosis/occlusion; both risk rupture or tissue death.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely explanation?
One set of risk factors, two arterial outcomes: dilate or narrow.

elim: Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos cause young-onset aneurysm, not occlusive disease in a smoker.
Possible, but claudication suggests chronic atherosclerotic occlusion.
An aneurysm does not steal blood from the leg arteries.
No features of vasculitis are present.

steps.x: Same risk factors, different responses: aneurysm (dilation) vs occlusion (stenosis).
